blocks.text: 20-FIN / finance and accounting Goes here. An interview with an accounting integrator detailing the specific rules for calculating Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) in e-commerce, including how to handle freight, duties, drop-shipping fees, customer returns, packaging, and Amazon/Shopify platform fees. Not here. • Negotiating freight or finding manufacturing suppliers -> 18-COG • Product pricing strategy and ad copy -> 03-OFF

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides explicit, practical guidance on how e-commerce brands must classify operational expenses versus Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) to accurately track gross margins and profitability. modules: [FIN] topics: [COGS, e-commerce accounting, freight classification, landed cost, gross margin, inventory management, drop shipping, customs duties] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. defining COGS / defining Cost of Goods Sold as every expense incurred to bring a product up to the point it sits on the warehouse shelf ready to sell ("all in until it's in"); freight and duty classification / clarifying that inbound freight, shipping container costs, and customs tariffs are strictly included in COGS; outbound shipping classification / noting that outbound shipping to the customer is an operating expense unless it's a drop-shipping model or explicitly baked into a "free shipping" retail price; packaging classification / distinguishing between "product packaging" (the retail box sitting on the shelf), which is COGS, and the "shipping packaging" (the brown cardboard box), which is an operating expense; platform fees / explicitly stating that Amazon PPC fees, Shopify transaction fees, advertising, and warehouse rent (3PL storage) are operating expenses, not COGS; returns accounting / explaining that the cost of shipping a return back is an overhead expense, but the cost to repackage or refurbish the item to make it sellable again can be classified as COGS; inventory management / recommending software over spreadsheets to automatically attribute and weight lump-sum freight and duty invoices down to the individual SKU level to calculate true landed cost.

The "All in until it's in" Rule: The guiding accounting principle that any cost incurred before the product is ready to be sold on the shelf is COGS, and any cost incurred after the sale is an operating expense.

The Packaging Distinction: The specific rule that the retail box (e.g., the white Apple iPhone box) is part of COGS, but the brown cardboard shipping box it goes into for delivery is a shipping expense.

The Drop-Shipping Exception: Noting that outbound shipping is usually an expense, except in drop-shipping models where the supplier charges the merchant a bundled outbound freight fee, which is then counted as COGS.

The Repackaging Rule for Returns: Clarifying that return shipping is an overhead expense, but the labor and materials used to repackage that returned item to make it sellable again are classified as COGS.
Skip. Plugs for the A2X software tool and Outserve accounting services.
Scope mix. 100% baseline (standard accounting and reporting principles). Volume. ~350 words.

everyone and welcome. Today we're diving into the world of COGS. That's cost of goods sold. So, before we get into the nuts and bolts of cost of goods sold, let's talk about why it's important to get it right in the first place. Why is close enough not good enough for e-commerce brands? Um, Phil, you tell us a bit more about that. >> I think, you know, for us, it it we talk about COGS all the time, but what we're really talking about is margin and profit. And of course hopefully that's what all the all the businesses uh are are in this in this for um especially in these you know challenging challenging times. Um, if you don't know your cogs, then you don't know your your profit margin. You you can't calculate your profit. And and I think, you know, when we think about strategy and and all businesses need to be thinking about their strategy so much at the time once you've decided what problem you're solving, you know, what great product you've got, then your cost of goods sold and your margin is really going to dictate so much of your strategy from what channels you sell on, how you promote. um it's it's really going to be the anchor of of everything in in your business uh to understand how you're going to going to make money, how you're going to be profitable, how you're going to be successful and and deliver maximum value. Um and you know, it feels to me so many times that businesses without understanding COGS are really flying blind, flying by the seat of their pants and and uh understandably giving themselves some sleepless nights maybe. >> Yes, I can imagine. So um okay so from the accounting side just tell us to start with what exactly does cost of goods sold cover and how would you go about calculating it? Yeah. And I think we could all say straight away, Ellsworth, it's complicated. It's it's complex. It's not always straightforward. And for different businesses, it it can be quite different. I think if we just try and focus at the moment on on many of the types of businesses that we would uh have as as A2X clients who are buying products in and selling products, we can touch a bit, you know, obviously if you're manufacturing, then your cost of goods sold is going to have another layer and level to it. Um, you know, think from the supplier door onto your shelf um before it's sold. It might be, you know, sometimes even for some some of our clients that's not clear and until it's uh later on prices fluctuate and change, especially in some commodity markets, currencies change. But then, of course, the big ones we often think about is freight. It's the freight cost to bring that product in. And then of course you're going to have to think about how do you actually allocate that that complete container cost to each product. Um duties uh is is another one that we we spend a lot of time thinking about. you know a lot of discussion on on tariffs at the moment and and that affects everybody. So, it's increasing that uh that that product product cost and and anything really to get it into your warehouse onto your shelf is going to be included in there. Um, so I think that's that's really the starting point, but also it's not just okay, what's in there then how how is it calculated? because you might have that those duties and those freight in sort of big lumps on invoices from different people and then it's all got to be attributed across essentially down to a unit by by unit cost. And of course at every level we can get a little bit more complicated. >> You know in when we've got clients in fashion and apparel then they can have a lot of returns and many businesses can have returns and then when stuff comes back in you've got to start understanding the cost there. If if the if the cost is actually to repackage that product into that maybe to make it sellable again, that could be part of the cost of goods sold. If it's part of bringing it back and then actually then just getting it ready to to ship it out again, then that's not. So, you know, there's those that fine line between there's lots of costs going on and just really understanding which which part of of it is it is it to get it ready up to that to sell it and then it's a co cost after sale and that's what you've you've got to think sometimes is really the the shipping cost to send it out is after you've sold it. >> Yes. >> Um the brown box that it goes in is a cost after you sold it. the, you know, the product box was a cost before you sold it and and start to think about things. There's a few little rules that you can follow as in would you have incurred this cost anyway if you hadn't have bought that item. So, it's a bit like the rent of your warehouse. You would have incurred that cost whatever. Even if you didn't buy that shipment, you would have still had that cost. So, it's it's expense after it's got in again. All in until it's in, it's in. Supplier discounts or credits. >> Um, yeah, I think, you know, it depends. I'd say generally speaking if a supplier has given you a discount on a product that you are you are buying then that's in in cost of goods sold. So it's reduced the cost. Um obviously if they're giving you a credit depends what they've given you a credit might be that you've given them the stock back. So we're going to have the stock movement anyway. So we got movement in stock and there's a credit note from that. I would say generally speaking um we'd we'd be looking at cost of goods sold from those supplier costs. >> Okay. There is no doubt some interesting KPIs that different businesses can have and definitely we see this in apparel businesses that they they will have a look at slightly different margin figures as well as cost of goods sold, gross profit margin. We can have sort of contribution margin. We can have some really interesting stats on returns understanding what it's cost on that. But really strictly speaking for statutory accounts then it's you know there's a distinction between the cost to return the goods in and anything you need to do to get the cost the goods ready to sell them again. >> Yeah. Um, and actually making sure that that there is there is a sale. Yeah, I think we we're seeing it's harder and harder to offer, you know, free postage and free returns, which of course is cutting into your profits significantly. And this again is the key reporting everybody needs to know. COGS margin very important, but we need to consider all of the the cost of doing business and and how that affects profitability. >> Yeah, 100%. Okay, great. So, that's been brilliant. Phil, >> um obviously I'm I'm a little bit biased and when we really need to, you know, those businesses have the best calculations they can is is probably having inventory management software. But actually, I'm actually going to start catch capturing freight and duty costs actually relevant to those products. Um, what we've seen businesses, you know, do over over the time is sort of just have a pile of freight and duty invoices and then actually never quite work out what products were they for. You know, best practice is capture those freight costs, those duty costs and any other relevant costs at at the right point attributed to the right purchases. And that can be challenging. You could definitely try and do that in a spreadsheet, but I think as the business scales and grows, you need software that's going to help you actually calculate the the the landed cost by really giving you the the system and the process to attribute those those additional costs and sometimes again they need to be weighted across. You could have ordered three or four things and that duty or the freight cost needs to be weighted or attributed differently across those and that and that's where you know some of this great software can really help. >> Okay, that's that's really helpful.
